LLM routing and expert finding share a premise: capability is
query-dependent, so a dispatcher should match the question to the candidate
rather than rely only on a global winner. They diverge in what the dispatcher
can observe and what it must optimize. TREC 2026 requires a complete ranking of
150 fixed candidate IDs without live test-time calls. Many routing papers choose
one model from a smaller menu, inspect current outputs, or trade quality against
cost and latency.

## Evidence ideas that transfer

Classical expert finding supplies the most direct structural analogy. Balog,
Azzopardi, and de Rijke distinguish candidate profiles from an evidence-first
document model: retrieve relevant work samples, associate them with experts,
then aggregate. Macdonald and Ounis compare voting and score fusion, while
ReDDE estimates a resource's relevant-document mass. Together they motivate
response retrieval, score normalization, capped aggregation, and uncertainty
gates when local evidence is diffuse.

Modern routing expands the feature space. RouterBench organizes historical
query-by-model outcomes so routers can learn complementarity. RouteLLM learns
from preference data. GraphRouter represents query, task, and model
relationships explicitly. ContextualRouter retrieves similar past queries,
which closely resembles the current dense-neighbor control. FrugalGPT and
LLM-Blender support cascades or output comparison, but depend on actions and
objectives that the track does not expose.

The broader evidence also protects simple baselines. LLMRouterBench reports
that sophisticated routers can be difficult to distinguish from simpler
alternatives under unified evaluation. That supports an experiment ladder:
global prior, sparse and dense similar-query retrieval, response retrieval,
query-candidate interactions, then learned or graph-based fusion. Complexity
earns a role only if it improves held-out query groups over those controls.

## What does not transfer

Published routing gains are not expected TREC gains. Candidate count, model
identity, available outputs, cost objective, labels, and data split can all
differ. Live-output selection and cost thresholds are especially incompatible
with a no-test-time-call, full-ranking task. The literature proposes evidence
signals; only current, query-grouped development evaluation can establish local
utility, and it still cannot establish hidden-test performance.
